cover.html:
- Welcome — this briefing is about Elastic entering the fastest-growing segment in observability: metrics.
- Not a roadmap story. This is GA, in production, with benchmarks to back it.
- Three things to take away today: the architecture is new, the performance is best-in-class, and the migration friction is gone.
launch.html:
- The headline: Observability Metrics is GA. June 29, 2026.
- Our philosophy: engineers don't change tools — we meet them where they are.
- Three numbers to remember: 30× faster queries than Prometheus. 4× lower TCO than Datadog. Zero dashboard rewrites.
- Grafana dashboards, PromQL queries, alerting rules — all kept. Elastic just becomes the backend underneath.
what-are-metrics.html:
- Quick level-set before the architecture story. Metrics are what wake engineers up at 3am — the highest-frequency signal in observability.
- Three primitives, unchanged since Prometheus: counters only go up, gauges snapshot a point in time, histograms give you p50/p95/p99 from one metric.
- Every alert that fires, every dashboard that renders — it's these three types underneath.
- Hold onto that: three simple types. The next slide shows what AI does to them.
ai-metrics.html:
- Same three types — but AI changes the volume equation completely.
- COUNTER (agent_tool_calls_total): one user query triggers an unknown number of tool calls. Each invocation adds to the count — a staircase that climbs as the agent works. The total is unpredictable until the session ends.
- GAUGE (active_agent_loops): how deep is the agent looping right now? Unlike a web request with a fixed call stack, agents recurse, retry, and branch. Tracking live loop depth is a new instrumentation problem that traditional observability never had to handle.
- HISTOGRAM (tool_response_duration_seconds): web search, code execution, database queries — each tool has its own latency distribution and p50/p95/p99. One histogram per tool type, and agents use many tools. That cardinality alone multiplies your series count.
- The explosion: each AI session spawns new metric dimensions — agent ID, model version, tool name, retry count. As adoption scales, the series count explodes. Most standard metric stores charge per series.
- The blindness risk: incident investigation depends on the full chain of events across every agent call, tool invocation, and model response. Drop a metric series — even one — and you lose the thread. Missing data is not a gap; it is a blind spot that makes RCA impossible.
- These two problems — cost and blindness — are why the architecture had to change.
what-changed.html:
- The setup: metrics were already voluminous before AI. Now AI causes an explosion, and that means a cost issue and an efficiency problem.
- Especially for vendors who price on custom metrics — Datadog being the clearest example — the AI era magnifies the unit economics problem dramatically. Every new agent dimension is a new billable series.
- Grafana/Mimir is more efficient but the operational burden is high. Elastic is more efficient than both and operationally simpler.
- This is causing real pain for customers — and pain creates appetite. We are hearing from customers who are actively looking.
- Our answer on storage: TSDS is purpose-built time-series storage — automatic rollup, downsampling, compression. 6.6× more efficient than index-based storage.
- Our answer on migration: full PromQL in Kibana, Grafana-compatible. Existing dashboards, queries, and alerting rules work without modification. Zero migration tax.
- Our answer on scale: 160× faster queries, handles millions of active series. Metrics are signals for AI operations, not isolated data.
doc-store.html:
- This slide is a standalone celebration of the doc store — do not frame it as a 'before.' Elastic's document store is still the right architecture for logs. This is not a history lesson.
- How it works: any log line — JSON, syslog, unstructured app log — comes in. Fields are extracted automatically, regardless of schema. An inverted index is built: 'ERROR' maps to doc0, doc3, doc7... 'payment-svc' maps to doc0, doc1, doc2... Any new field is indexed automatically — no schema migration, no DDL.
- Why this beats ClickHouse for logs: Elastic does MATCH and SCORE. ClickHouse does match but not score, and its match on unstructured data is significantly slower. Application logs — arbitrary schema, constantly evolving — are where Elastic is untouchable. Most engineering teams will never put application logs into ClickHouse. ClickHouse works on standardized structured logs; it doesn't handle the messy reality of app logs.
- The main point to land: Elastic made inverted indexes work at log scale. That is real engineering. You do not need to apologize for this architecture — it is genuinely great at what it does.
columnar-intro.html:
- Let this one land on its own: 25 bytes per data point down to 3.75.
- The transition line into this slide, spoken over the doc-store slide: 'Now, what happens when you put a metric into that document store? A metric is tiny — a timestamp, a value, a few dimensions. But the doc store wraps it in machinery built for documents: an _id, sequence numbers, inverted index entries, per-field metadata. You are storing all that metadata for something so small. And reading it back means scanning the full document — effectively a full table scan.'
- Then this number lands: we got it down to 3.75 bytes per point. (Slide auto-advances into the columnar engine slide.)
columnar.html:
- This slide mirrors the doc-store slide deliberately: logs are messy and schemaless, so we built an engine that extracts and indexes everything. Metrics are the opposite — tiny, identical, relentless — so we built the opposite engine.
- The mechanism: each field is its own column on disk. avg(cpu_usage) touches the cpu_usage column and nothing else — one sequential pass, zero wasted reads. That is a column-based read instead of a full-document scan. That is why columnar is so great for time-series, well-structured data. Physics, not caching tricks.
- DIM filters: proprietary IP. Dimension-aware skip filters pushed down to the storage layer — non-matching blocks are skipped before they are ever decoded. The audience does not need to understand what a DIM filter is; they need to register that Elastic has built something special here. Just say it: this is significant IP.
- Why faster than ClickHouse, who is also columnar? ClickHouse is a full BI engine — all of SQL, joins, OLAP. That generality has a cost on every query. Our engine does one thing: time-series. Purpose-built beats general-purpose in its own domain.
- How storage reached 3.75 bytes per point (from the engineering deep-dive, for questions): doc-value skippers replace inverted indices and BKD trees, giving true columnar files; synthetic _id (tsid + timestamp) means the _id is computed, not stored; trimmed sequence numbers; numeric codecs with 512-byte blocks tuned for dimension patterns like IP addresses; shard routing and index sort on _tsid keeps each series sequential on disk so codecs and skippers stay effective.
- How queries got fast (same source): the TS command aggregates per time series then groups — expresses time-series math in one ES|QL pipeline; sorted _tsid + time enables vectorized, parallel, sequential column reads; zero-copy primitive blocks; time and dimension filters pushed down to Lucene skippers; RATE() computed on ordered slices with correct counter-reset handling.
- On ingest: be honest. Prometheus/Glyphos is approximately 10-20% faster at ingest than we are. Saying this buys credibility — then you explain that query and storage are where the cost and pain live, and there we lead by a wide margin.
- For the full technical detail, reference the architectural improvements and benchmark comparison blog (Alex Batsakis's team).
benchmarks.html:
- The claim to open with, per Ash: we built the best data store for logs. We believe we have now done it for metrics.
- The question this slide preempts: 'how did you become 30× faster than Prometheus? What did you do?' Every number has its how on the slide. Be ready to go one level deeper on each.
- Queries (30× vs Prometheus and Mimir; up to 8× vs ClickHouse on gauges, 3.5× on counter rates): series sorted on disk by _tsid then time; one column read; DIM filters and doc-value skippers eliminate non-matching blocks before they are decoded; single vectorized aggregation pass (the TS command in ES|QL). Concrete anchor on the slide: 4 hours over 1.4M series in under 2s vs over 30s for Prometheus.
- Storage (3.75 bytes per point, 6.7× vs ES 8.x, 2.5× vs Prometheus, 2× vs ClickHouse): store less, compute the rest. Synthetic _id derived from tsid + timestamp instead of stored; doc-value skippers replace inverted indices and BKD trees; trimmed sequence numbers; numeric codec blocks widened from 128 to 512 elements to catch repeating dimension patterns like IPs.
- Ingest: parity with Prometheus and Mimir (the benchmark actually shows us slightly ahead, by a small margin), 1.4× faster than ClickHouse. Do not oversell this one; conceding it is the credibility play. How: native OTLP protobuf parsing (cheaper than JSON), _tsid hash computed once per batch and amortized, synthetic recovery source halves ingest disk IO.
- Methodology if pressed: default configurations for every system (Prometheus v3.11.1, Mimir v3.0.6, ClickHouse v26.3), open-source workload generator (metricsgenreceiver, inspired by TSBS), disclosed EC2 hardware, single-node. Multi-node scale-out results are planned for a future post.
- Caveat to volunteer if asked about ClickHouse queries: ClickHouse lacks native time-series aggregations and counter-reset detection, so those comparisons are directional.
- Source: Elastic Search Labs blog, 'Elasticsearch columnar metrics engine: 30x faster than Prometheus'.
one-platform.html:
- This is the slide Santosh asked for: single platform, yet optimized per signal. The third repetition of the visual pattern (doc store slide, columnar slide, now this) is deliberate: we keep building the right engine for each signal, and the user never feels the seams.
- The routing point: depending on the signal, Elasticsearch uses a different index type automatically. Nobody configures 'send logs here, metrics there.' It just happens. Zero config.
- The three engines: document store (match and score for logs), columnar store (one column read for metrics), vector store (semantic similarity for meaning: incident reports, runbooks, embeddings).
- The payoff on the right: one question touches all three. 'Why is checkout slow?' correlates a metric spike (columnar), the error logs (doc store), and a similar past incident with a documented fix (vector). No other platform answers that in one query, because signals live in separate products with separate query languages.
- Ash's framing to carry verbally: this is super cool because it is the same query mechanism, same dashboards, everything, and each signal is hyper optimized underneath.
- This leads into the next slide: the platform is the foundation, and on top of it we ship a full solution for metrics, not just a data store.
offering.html:
- What's actually in the box at GA — three pillars.
- Fully functional: PromQL support covering 90%+ of Grafana dashboards natively, full alerting compatibility, every metric type, downsampling and rollup out of the box.
- Rich content: 1,000+ OOTB dashboards, 300+ integrations, native OTel ingestion, Prometheus remote write.
- Kibana becomes a real metrics UI — no Grafana dependency required, but Grafana still works if that's what the team wants.
- The point: this is not a v1. It's a complete offering on day one.
promql.html:
- 80% of enterprise SREs already speak PromQL. That's their language — we didn't ask them to learn ours.
- 90% of queries in the top 100 Grafana dashboards execute natively in Kibana today.
- No plugins, no adapters, no translation layer — it runs wherever ES|QL runs.
- The framing: everything they know, everything they've built — same queries, up to 30× faster.
migrate.html:
- Migration risk is the objection that kills platform deals. This neutralizes it.
- Three steps: connect your Datadog org or Grafana instance, automatic conversion of dashboards and alert rules, go live in Kibana.
- Same day. Not a quarter-long professional services engagement — overnight.
- Team keeps their workflows. The backend changes; their muscle memory doesn't.
kubernetes.html:
- The promise: a lovable out-of-the-box experience — value before configuration.
- We start with Kubernetes because that's where the market is: 93% of companies are running or evaluating it. (Source: CNCF 2024 Annual Cloud Native Survey — use/pilot/evaluate combined; production use alone was 80%, and the 2025 survey puts production at 82%.)
- Out of the box: revamped dashboards and alerts, OOTB SLOs, enhanced OTel experience, agent skills for K8s workflows.
- No instrumentation project. No dashboard-building sprint. It's just there on day one.
- And Kubernetes is the starting point, not the boundary — the same OOTB bar applies across the portfolio.
plain-english.html:
- This is where the metrics story connects to the AI story.
- Native MCP server — any Claude-compatible client connects straight to the Elastic cluster.
- Skills load automatically: RCA, anomaly detection, remediation. Results render as rich cards, not raw JSON.
- Your systems become conversational. Ask in plain English, get answers in plain English — inside the agents and workflows teams already use.
mcp-demo.html:
- The framing on this one matters: engineers already live in an agent. We don't pull them into another tool — we meet them in theirs.
- The demo plays by itself — the chat drives the app. Watch the sequence: connect to the cluster, and six observability skills load automatically from the MCP server. That's the injection story: no custom engineering per use case, skills are discovered at handshake.
- Then the conversation: health summary, ML-scored anomaly explorer, root-cause drill-down, blast radius — each question renders live in the panel.
- No dashboard hunting, no query writing, no context switch. 'What's wrong with my cluster?' — and it answers with data.
- This is shipping, not a concept demo. (Arrow keys skip/rewind if you need to pace it.)
gtm.html:
- The frame, per Ash: it's as simple as this. We have a great position in logs. Some of the largest customers in the world depend on us for logs. They all have very expensive metric solutions, and there is real openness to something more efficient and integrated. That's our play.
- Land and expand is the headline motion (Santosh): logs are landed, metrics is the expansion. The low-hanging fruit is our existing Log Analytics customers; we go to all of them.
- Do not oversell (Navam): this slide explains the go-to-market motion; it does not promise revenue upside. Expect the question 'will this be material for you this year?' Steer to the motion: we are explaining how we take it to market, the installed base gives us distribution, and adoption compounds from there. Do not commit to a revenue number.
- Also per Navam: do not be shy about lower TCO. Say it plainly and with confidence.
- Play one, expand: navigate to the metrics buyer inside the existing account. Same platform, one bill, no new vendor review.
- Play two, consolidate: Prometheus, Mimir, and Grafana shops keep their PromQL, dashboards, and alerting rules — and pick their on-ramp. Elastic as a faster engine under their existing Grafana, or the full move to Kibana with native PromQL. Either way, logs and metrics converge on one platform.
- Play three, displace: price-sensitive accounts at renewal time. IT budgets are stretched — CIOs want to save without sacrificing coverage. 4× lower TCO than Datadog, automated conversion, live the same day. (No need to name the vendor on the slide — the room knows.)
- The sequencing is deliberate: expand the base first, consolidate open-source sprawl, then displace on renewal cycles.
close.html:
- Five reasons this market is ours to take — the summary slide for your notes.
- Performance at scale: 30× queries, 6.6× storage, on a proven engine.
- Zero migration friction: PromQL-native, Grafana-compatible, hours not months.
- Unified platform: metrics next to logs, traces, synthetics. One query language, one bill.
- AI-ready by design: the same platform that runs Elastic nightshift. Metrics feed the AI SRE — they're not isolated data.
- Happy to go deeper on any of these. Thank you.
thank-you.html:
- Thank you for the time today.
- Three takeaways: the architecture is genuinely new, the benchmarks lead the market, and the migration friction is gone.
- Questions welcome — and everything we covered is at elastic.co/observability. Let's keep the conversation going.
